en: Your dear elder Jakyp's
Heart was at ease toward the people;
Of Altai's Manchus and Kalmyks,
Jakyp was richer than all.
His wealth became known to the people;
Esenkan was their ruler,
And he was entered in his register.
His name reached Alay,
The name of your champion elder Jakyp.
His fame spread among the people;
He grew rich in countless livestock,
Writing documents, receiving letters,
He was called Jakyp the Rich.
His livestock filled the pasture;
To the many people of Altai,
Your champion named Jakyp
Had come to seem a saint.
Famous Jakyp grew rich,
But for many years
He longed for a single child.
“I have raised livestock, but have no child;
Much I ask of the Creator—
I have no power to beget a child.
My mountain horses number nine san,
There is no dappled one among my fine steeds.
Wretched livestock amassed for torment!
To receive them,
In this world of torment I have no child.
Fine horses and steeds have no sense,
There is no master to receive them!
What God has done,
I have no choice but to bear.
Wretched livestock without an owner,
I have no child to receive them.
I amassed much empty worldly wealth,
Yet have no power to beget a child.
Amassing so much worldly wealth,
Shall I thus attain a legacy?
My gelded camels number six san;
Wandering childless,
Such a man your Jakyp has become.
Ownerless livestock amassed in vain—
To share them, I have no son;
My living soul reels.
The precious stock have filled the dwelling,
But there is no son to carry on my line;
My precious life can bear no more.
Camels and elephants carry my loads;
That wife I married, Chyyrdy,
It has been many years since I wed her.
She does not let down and comb her hair;
May she wither—what days are these?!
Baatyrkan's daughter Bakdöölöt
Was my wife from the beginning.
Though I cherish her, she bears no child;
This has become the greatest misery!
Raising so much ownerless livestock,
Ah,
I shall attain a legacy—
With no child to rely on,
Shall I pass away without an heir?!
I raised argymaks that have no sense;
There is no master to tend and ride them!
Since I came to Altai,
I have amassed much wretched livestock,
But never led a child to the place of honor,
Nor heard its little cry.
My sorrow is great, my heart a coal;
I have no swift steed to ride in Altai,
Born of the same nest as me,
My eight exiled brothers are not here,
My heart is grief, my breast a coal.
To enjoy the fruits of my livestock,
I have no brave Kyrgyz people;
When I bow down, I have no people;
To graze the ownerless livestock,
I have no ancient homeland.
This wretched people in Altai—
When I bow down, I have no people;
Let alone my people, here
I have no sister's son for company.
No elder brother stands before me;
I made my living here in Altai,
With no mother's brother to support me.
My abundant wealth is beyond counting;
Asking for food, never sated,
Never giving up their hunger for more—
My lion-hearted Kyrgyz people are not here!
The turmoil God has laid on me,
I have no choice but to bear.
I amassed much ownerless livestock,
I have no child to receive it.
We have become forty Kyrgyz households;
Among the Black Kalmyks and Manchus
We stand,
With no means to find our people.
People, what course shall we take?
Among these Kalmyks,
Will your elder Jakyp die?
Saying, ‘Jakyp had no child,’
The great forsaken herds—
Will Kalmyk monks come and divide them?
Will their village headman inflict humiliation?
We were a people oppressed from the first;
These forsaken herds—
Will your Chinese take possession of them?
At the tent with copper pillars,
There is no one to answer back
To this Black Kalmyk warrior!
O Baltay, the hawthorn-hafted axe,
Who will fit it without twisting it?
This many people waiting here,
Who will lead them without leaving them forlorn?
O Baltay, the black-cheeked axe,
Who will fit it without tilting it?
The great people held in confinement,
Who will lead them without causing grief?”
Lamenting, “I have no child,”
Your rich Jakyp said these words.
His whole inside burned with fire;
He earnestly prayed for a child.
Even so he had seen no child;
Yet Jakyp did not die of shame.
When Jakyp voiced his sorrow,
The forty Kyrgyz households wept.
Khan Jakyp's countless livestock
Overflowed like grass in spring.
Tears flowing from both eyes
Of dear old Jakyp
Ran down both his cheeks.
His whole being crushed,
Your rich Jakyp, that brave man,
Asked the Lord for a child.
Let us leave him there;
From that paradise-like city of Beijing,
Whose ruler was Esenkan,
Let us now begin the news.
In the kakan's Beijing
Was the renowned Esenkan.
The afflictions of six years ahead,
Who could think and know them today—
He had such a sorcerer.
A diviner casting lots,
Wearing a malakay cap,
The troubles of seven years
He could fully think out and know,
His herald who spoke plainly,
His sorcerer, his diviner.
Do not ask about Beijing;
Beijing is no common place,
The Chinese no simple people.
Back in the time of Prophet Noah,
The Flood came then.
When the Flood surged and overflowed,
When it covered the whole world,
Laying it waste,
Great sorrow remained in the heart;
The surging Flood could not reach it,
And nine hundred households remained there.
When the pure Prophet Muhammad
Ascended to the heavenly throne,
On Beijing, where light was shed,
No one cast a glance,
No mighty one called it to account.
While the Prophet lived,
In this very Beijing
Many different peoples remained.
When they waged holy war on unbelievers,
The khan of Chin-Machin,
When they went saying, “I will seize him,”
They married women in Beijing
And remained there, the Turkana;
If we truly seek, we shall find them,
The Dungans, true Muslims.
You may tell of them without regret:
True descendants of the Kyrgyz,
In the Beijing of Chin-Machin
A people called Salalyk remained.
In knowing the ways of peoples,
Esenkan was outstanding.
His forefather was Chylaba;
He had a splendid city he founded,
The afflictions of seven years,
Who could know them in seven days—
He had seven such magicians too.
His sorcerer learned of it;
Into Esenkan's presence
He came causing an uproar.
Before Esenkan
Stood a tower for keeping watch.
Do not ask about the tower—
Ninety thousand fathoms high!
The bell upon that tower—
Its bell was bronze and copper,
Three fathoms in girth;
If you hear its voice, flee far away.
The signaling bell—
When they struck its bell once,
Such was Esenkan's knowledge—
Six days' journey away
It could be heard with ease,
The reach of this unbeliever.
A light was lit upon the tower,
The bell was loudly struck.
When they heard the bell,
All the sorcerers gathered.
Taking the Iliyi book in hand,
He saw within the book:
“With a face like buttered wheat,
With eyes like twilight mist,
With the look of a hungry lion,
The famous Khan Manas will arise;
His wrath will drive the life from men.
He will be born among the Burut;
When Manas mounts a horse,
Your Torgut will be utterly slaughtered.
Of middle height, broad-shouldered,
Khan Manas will arise from the Kyrgyz;
His wrath will drive the life from men.
Born with all his world in balance,
The lion Manas will be born among the Burut;
His movement raises dust,
His voice drives life from men.
A hero like a lion will be born,
A man who overturns the world will be born.
When that Manas is born,
Eighty-four are fully armed;
Wherever he strikes is red fire.
If Manas is born and grows,
He will surely bring us no good;
He will not leave this Beijing intact.
Our forefather Chylaba!
That accursed one's valor
Will ravage the world,
Such is Manas's lion might.
Never sated when he drinks blood,
He is the man who will wreak havoc,
Sparing no one who wrestles him.
He will lay your khan waste,
Bewilder every one of you,
Make your souls shriek.
He will smash to pieces
The support on which you rely;
He will drench in red blood
These Chinese people of yours.
Your rulers, your khan—
The hero Manas will arise among the Burut
And trample your city of Beijing.
If that Manas is born,
He will turn white deer into cattle;
This very Beijing
He will ravage time and again.
He will chase blue-gray deer and make them cattle;
Beyond Beijing, that Manas
Will ravage every place he sees.
He will leave nothing of twelve peoples;
